revisions.title: A question that returns to Meno
revisions.body: Meno asks whether virtue is taught, practiced, or natural. Socrates contrasts Thessalian confidence, linked to Gorgias, with Athenian ignorance, then argues that knowing what virtue is precedes knowing what sort of thing it is. When Meno invokes Gorgias, Socrates says he cannot presently recall how Gorgias struck him. The passage leaves the lapse's sincerity open and returns the question to Meno.

revisions.title: A definition must start somewhere shared
revisions.body: Socrates turns the demand for a definition into a rehearsal. One way to read Meno’s objection is that the first proposal makes shape depend on color: someone who does not know color has learned nothing about shape. That is a failure of explanatory starting point, not a demonstrated proof of circularity. Socrates then shifts to terms Meno says he knows—end, limit, plane, and solid—and proposes shape as the limit of a solid.

revisions.title: Aporia before the diagonal
revisions.body: Socrates turns the doubled square into a test of how inquiry begins. The boy answers confidently—first that the side should double, then that it should be three feet—but the resulting areas are sixteen and nine, not eight. Questioning continues toward the diagonal only after this confidence has failed. One way to read the episode is as a miniature parallel to the dialogue’s larger inquiry, not as an exact repetition of Meno’s experience.

revisions.title: The conditional inference: virtue as wisdom
revisions.body: Socrates makes “beneficial” depend on guidance: health, wealth, courage, and temperance can help or harm according to whether wisdom governs their use. On premises Meno has accepted, he therefore infers that virtue is a kind of wisdom. Read this as a conditional argumentative result, not as a settled conclusion about how virtue is acquired.

revisions.title: The inference from no teachers
revisions.body: Socrates turns a dispute about expertise into a test of teachability. Because neither the sophists nor the respected men can count as teachers of virtue, he and Meno infer that there can be no students—and therefore no teachable virtue. The conclusion is unsettling: Meno immediately asks how good people arise at all.
